extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates / graduate students in algebraic geometry (Math 216)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and states standard definitions, theorems, and exercise-guided criteria from a foundations-level algebraic geometry textbook (Math 216), focusing on numerical properties of line bundles, Serre duality, Hilbert polynomials, degree/genus, and cohomological characterizations of ampleness/affineness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nefness of an invertible sheaf (nef)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invertible sheaf L is numerically effective (nef) if for every integral curve C in X, deg_C L ≥ 0 (Definition 18.4.11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks and exercises: nefness is a numerical property; equivalently deg_C L ≥ 0 for all integral curves C (18.4.V(a)). Pullback preserves nefness: if π : X → Y is proper and L is nef on Y, then π^*L is nef on X (18.4.V(b)). L is nef iff it is nef on each irreducible component (18.4.V(c)). The nef elements of Pic X form a semigroup (18.4.V(d)). Ample invertible sheaves are nef (18.4.V(e)). L is nef iff L^{⊗n} is nef for n ∈ Z_{≥0} (18.4.V(f)). Exercises extend to Q-line bundles and the nef cone (18.4.W).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nef cone / nef Q-line bundles
rubrics_metrics.description: The nef Q-line bundles form a closed cone in N1_Q(X); this cone is called the nef cone (Exercise 18.4.W).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/explanation: boundaries of the nef cone correspond to linear series that give contractions (exercise 18.4.X for P^2_k and P^1_k × P^1_k). The ample cone is contained in the nef cone and (for projective X) is its interior (Kleiman's criterion referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ampleness depends only on numerical class in N1_Q(X)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an invertible sheaf L is ample depends only on its class in N1_Q(X), i.e., on its intersections with curves; one can define ampleness for Q-line bundles accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: ample divisors form a cone in N1_Q(X); by Kleiman's numerical criterion (Theorem 20.4.6) the ample divisors are precisely the interior of the nef cone when X is projective. Also L is ample iff L^{⊗n} is ample for n∈Z_{>0} (as for nefness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Picard number and finiteness of N1(X)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define NS(X) = Pic X modulo algebraic equivalence; the Néron–Severi Theorem (Theorem of the Base) states NS(X) is finitely generated. The group N1(X) = Pic X / Pic^τ X is a quotient of NS(X) and hence finitely generated; being abelian and torsion-free it is a finite free Z-module. The rank is the Picard number ρ(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ρ(P^n)=1 and ρ((P^1)^n)=n. Remarks point to proofs and references; an exercise shows finiteness of ρ(X) over C via H^2(X,Z) (18.4.U).

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre duality for smooth projective varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a geometrically irreducible smooth projective k-variety of dimension n, there is an invertible sheaf ω_X such that h^i(X,F) = h^{n-i}(X, ω_X ⊗ F^∨) for all i and all finite-rank locally free sheaves F (Theorem 18.5.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a perfect pairing Hi(X,F) × H^{n−i}(X, ω_X ⊗ F^∨) → H^n(X, ω_X) ≅ k (equation 18.5.1.1). The sheaf ω_X equals the canonical bundle K_X = det(Ω_{X/k}) (Remark 18.5.2); smoothness can be relaxed and dualizing sheaf formalism is discussed in later chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical (dualizing) sheaf identification
rubrics_metrics.description: The dualizing/invertible Serre-dualizing sheaf ω_X coincides with the canonical sheaf (canonical bundle) K_X, defined as the determinant of the cotangent bundle Ω_{X/k} (Remark 18.5.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This connects Serre duality to algebraic volume forms; further formalization deferred to later chapters (see Desideratum 30.1.1 and Chapter 30).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of vector bundles on P^1 (Grothendieck's theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any rank r vector bundle E on P^1_k splits as a direct sum E ≅ O(a_1) ⊕ ··· ⊕ O(a_r) for a unique nondecreasing sequence of integers a_1 ≤ ··· ≤ a_r (Theorem 18.5.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises: the a_i can be recovered from dim_k Hom(O(m), E) (18.5.C); the proof uses cohomology and induction (exercises 18.5.D–18.5.I). Remarks discuss generalizations (Horrocks' criterion) and counterexamples in higher dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert function and Hilbert polynomial
rubrics_metrics.description: For a coherent sheaf F on a projective k-scheme X ⊂ P^n, define h_F(m) := h^0(X, F(m)). The Euler characteristic χ(X, F(m)) is a polynomial p_F(m) (the Hilbert polynomial) of degree equal to dim Supp F, and for m≫0, h^0(X,F(m)) = p_F(m) (Theorem 18.6.1, Definition 18.6.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof ingredients: Serre vanishing, reduction to algebraically closed/infinite base field, use of associated points and slicing by hyperplanes; exercises show how to compute p_X for examples (projective space, hypersurfaces, Veronese embeddings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of a projective scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: For a projective k-scheme X of dimension n, the degree deg X is defined as the leading coefficient of the Hilbert polynomial p_X(m) times n! (section 18.6.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and properties: deg P^n = 1; degree of the dth Veronese embedding is d^n (Exercises 18.6.J, 18.6.O); degree is always an integer (exercise 18.6.G); degree of a hypersurface computed via p_H(m)=p_{P^n}(m)−p_{P^n}(m−d) (18.6.2.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bézout's theorem / degree multiplicativity for intersections
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a projective scheme of dimension ≥1 and H is a hypersurface not containing any associated points of X, then deg(H ∩ X) = (deg H)(deg X) (Exercise 18.6.K).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plane curve example: two plane curves of degrees m and n with no common components meet in mn points counted with multiplicity. Use the condition on associated points to avoid embedded components; exercises relate this to classical slicing definitions of degree (18.6.N).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic genus from Hilbert polynomial
rubrics_metrics.description: The arithmetic genus of a projective scheme X is 1 − p_X(0) = 1 − χ(X, O_X) (section 18.6.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For complex curves this recovers topological genus via h^0(ω_C)=g (Exercise 18.5.A). Example: a plane curve of degree d has h^1(C,O_C) = (d−1)(d−2)/2 (equation 18.6.6.1), giving genera 0,1,3,6,... for d=1,2,3,4,5,...

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre's cohomological criterion for ampleness
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Noetherian base A and proper A-scheme X, an invertible sheaf L is ample on X iff for every coherent sheaf F there exists n_0 such that for all n ≥ n_0, Hi(X, F ⊗ L^{⊗n}) = 0 for all i > 0 (Theorem 18.7.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem lists equivalent formulations of ampleness (labels (a)–(c) refer to Theorem 16.6.2). Proof uses that some power of L is very ample and Serre vanishing; exercises guide the construction of an N so that L^{⊗n} is globally generated for n≥N and then show global generation of twists of any coherent F for n≫0 (18.7.A–18.7.E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences / local criteria for ampleness
rubrics_metrics.description: Ampleness behaves well under reduction and decomposition: L is ample on X iff L|_{X_{red}} is ample (18.7.A); L is ample iff it is ample on each irreducible component (18.7.B). On a projective curve, a line bundle is ample iff it has positive degree on each component (18.7.C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints: filtration by powers of the ideal sheaf of X_{red} and use of cohomological vanishing arguments; reduction steps are standard in applying Serre's criterion to prove projectivity of proper curves (18.7.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre's cohomological characterization of affineness
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Noetherian separated scheme X, the following are equivalent: (a) X is affine; (b) for any quasi-coherent sheaf F on X, Hi(X,F)=0 for all i>0; (c) for any coherent ideal sheaf I on X, H^1(X,I)=0 (Theorem 18.7.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks: (a)⇒(b)⇒(c) are formal; the substance is (c)⇒(a). Analogue: Stein spaces in complex analytic geometry are characterized by vanishing of higher cohomology of coherent sheaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert polynomial detects equality of closed subschemes
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ⊂ Y ⊂ P^n are closed embeddings and p_X(m) = p_Y(m) for m≫0, then X = Y (Exercise 18.6.F(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the exact sequence 0 → I_{X/Y}(m) → O_Y(m) → O_X(m) → 0 and use that a coherent sheaf with zero Hilbert polynomial is zero; useful criterion to show two projective subschemes coincide by comparing Hilbert polynomials for large m.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connectedness of positive-dimensional complete intersections
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch/hint: show h^0(X, O_X) = 1; the argument is robust under field extension and shows geometric connectedness for experts. Related exercises show examples where connectedness fails and how that signals failure of Cohen–Macaulay property.
